extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of satirical/bawdy Renaissance prose (general readers, translators, literature students)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing humorous satirical prose in the vein of Rabelais: episodic narrative that skewers institutions and human foibles through exaggeration, bawdy/physical jokes, mock-erudition, wordplay, and staged practical jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity in speech / avoid rambling
rubrics_metrics.description: I hate a gibble-gabble and a rimble-ramble talk. I am for a man of brevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise, punchy delivery over long-winded lectures—long digressions weaken comic force. The skipper interrupts an overly long seller; Panurge values quick decisive action (e.g., throws the ram overboard 'without any further tittle-tattle'). Use compression to heighten surprise and comic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize institutions by exaggerated caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: The text repeatedly lampoons merchants, monks, lawyers, catchpoles, and other social types by amplifying their vices and absurdities (e.g., catchpoles who prosper by being thrashed; monks in kitchens; ostentatious merchants’ tall tales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target institutional hypocrisy with caricature and tall tale: attribute absurd customs, corrupt incentives, and ritualized behavior to social types to reveal their folly. Use mock-technical language, invented pedigrees, and grandiose claims to make satire clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bodily/scatological and physical humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent recourse to low/physical comedy and scatology: references to urine, dung, farting, drowning sheep, beating, bawdy nicknames, and descriptions of bodies and bodily functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not shy from coarse, bodily detail—scatological elements and physical gags are used deliberately to shock, amuse, and debase pretension. Combine grotesque imagery with moral or social critique for a Rabelaisian effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque hyperbole and abundance of marvelous claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants and narrators make outrageously grand claims (horns that will grow asparagus, sheep urine yielding saltpetre, linage from mythic rams), and actions escalate to extreme outcomes (entire flocks leaping to drown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use escalating hyperbole and impossible causal claims to produce comic astonishment and to satirize credulity. Let the absurdities accumulate until the reader perceives the parody or exposes gullibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful wordplay, kennings and inventive terms of endearment
rubrics_metrics.description: The island of Ennasin speaks with comic pet-names and pairings (my butter / my eggs, my shell / my oyster, pear & cheese marriages), inventing metaphorical couplings and bawdy nicknames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create fresh, surprising compounds and terms of address to generate humor; use metaphorical pairings and double-meanings (often sexualized) to lampoon social relations and produce rapid comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise, cross-dressing and mistaken identity as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes use disguised pages dressed as women who cause a lord to mistake them for ladies, producing embarrassment and comic refusal to kiss—comic situations arise from role-play and revealed imposture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage misrecognition, cross-dressing, and theatrical disguise to create awkward social moments and expose vanity. Timing of revelation (delayed unmasking) increases embarrassment and laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical jokes and staged spectacles for revenge or mockery
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of staged public spectacles (Villon’s devils with bells, Basche’s mock wedding to punish a catchpole) show organized theatrical pranks used as social punishment or amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design public, theatrical set-pieces—props, noise, timing, costuming, and a crowd—to turn private grievances into comic spectacle; coordinate participants to produce controlled chaos that humiliates the target while entertaining onlookers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-solemnity / learned pastiche to satirize pretension
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator and characters invoke Aristotle, Averroes, Latin phrases, and faux-legal/clerical forms to lend a pompous air that is then undercut by absurd content (e.g., pseudo-scholarly glosses, 'Matter of breviary').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the tone and citations of erudition only to subvert them with base or ridiculous material. The juxtaposition of high-register learned language with coarse subject matter creates ironic contrast and ridicule of pretension.
